title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1900–1960 · Hardened Oil: Normann’s Hydrogenation, Crisco and Unilever, Factory-Ship Whaling, the Palm Plantation, Manchurian Soy and Keys’s Hypothesis

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars for glycerine and fat

entries.label: The war for glycerine: whale oil as contraband
entries.loc: South Georgia and the North Sea
entries.hint: Glycerine, a by-product of splitting whale oil, goes into nitroglycerine and so into explosives, and the war made whale oil a strategic good. Britain, which controlled more than two thirds of whaling in the Falkland Islands Dependencies, stopped Norwegian sales to the Central Powers by refusing Norway coal; Germany offered up to £300 a ton against the £25 the Allies paid, and in 1916 Britain temporarily cancelled Norwegian licences in the Antarctic to prevent the sale of ‘contraband’. All restrictions on the catch were lifted by 1914, and 11,792 whales were killed at South Georgia in 1915–16; from 1904 to 1917 the total there was 175,250.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.345–346 (PDF pp.368–369). The price and catch figures are Ellis’s; he cites no source for them in the passage read.

entries.label: The second war for fats: rationing, soy margarine and the cut-off oilseeds
entries.hint: The Second World War repeated many features of the First: international arrangements to handle supplies failed to prevent distorted markets, old connections broken, and output cut in some countries and raised in others; by 1947 the world supply of fats and oils was reckoned 10 per cent below pre-war levels while demand had risen. Margarine was rationed. In the United States, with oilseed imports hard to get, the government pushed soybean growing and soy margarine replaced butter on most tables; in 1943 margarine fats were 50 per cent cottonseed oil, 40 per cent soybean oil and 7 per cent animal fat. Germany, Japan and others entered the Antarctic whaling race before the war closed it, killing 46,039 whales in 1937–38.
entries.note: SECONDARY (three works read): Hunt in van Stuyvenberg (ed.), Margarine (1969) ch.2 pp.79–80 (the 1947 supply figure); van Stuyvenberg ch.7 p.289 (the 1943 shares; rationing); Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.5 p.424 (soy margarine in the war); Ellis (1991) p.312 (46,039 whales in 1937–38).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The margarine tax and its repeal, Ottawa, the whaling convention, the olive council

entries.label: The 1902 amendment: ten cents a pound on coloured margarine
entries.hint: In 1902 an amendment to the 1886 Oleomargarine Act put a tax of 10 cents a pound on margarine artificially coloured to resemble butter, and cut the tax on uncoloured margarine to a nominal ¼ cent. Production dropped sharply and did not regain its 1901 level until 1910; the tax, as one source put it, ‘fired up the very illegal selling that it was supposed to prevent’, and the Commissioner put the tax evaded in 1914 at $15 million. Manufacturers answered by selling colouring in little bags and, in the 1920s, by using more groundnut and soybean oils, whose natural yellow was legal and so free of the high tax.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7, pp.287–288 (‘More far-reaching discriminations: 1902 and 1931’). Van Stuyvenberg’s 1931 provisions are in the next folio paragraph, not read here.

entries.label: An international whaling convention, 1931–1949
entries.hint: A Geneva convention of 1931 on whaling was amended in London in 1937 to set minimum sizes for blue, fin and humpback whales, a three-month season and inspectors on every factory ship; the right whale has been protected by international agreement since 1937. The International Whaling Commission was established in 1949 and Ellis calls it ‘a handmaiden of the whaling industry’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.294, 312 and 314 (PDF pp.317, 335, 337). The terms of the 1931 convention are only partly described in the passages read.

entries.label: Imperial Preference at Ottawa: oils and fats behind imperial tariffs
entries.hint: The years 1929 to 1933 were ones of reaction to the overproduction of oils and fats: a million more tons of oilseed crops were produced in the mid-1930s than in the previous decade, and whale oil output had doubled. Governments took protective action: the Imperial Preference of the 1932 Ottawa Agreements Act in the United Kingdom set off a chain reaction, with France raising her tariffs against oilseed products from outside her own empire.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Hunt, ‘The raw materials’, in van Stuyvenberg (ed.), Margarine (1969) ch.2 (pp.40–80), the passage on 1929–33. Hunt’s ‘one million more tons’ and the doubling of whale oil are his figures.

entries.label: Washington repeals the tax on coloured margarine
entries.hint: Under pressure from cottonseed and soybean growers, consumers, workers’ organisations and the reorganised margarine manufacturers, the House of Representatives repealed the tax on coloured margarine in 1949, by 152 votes to 140, and the Senate followed in 1950. The ban on colouring was swept from almost all state laws, the last being Wisconsin’s in 1967, and in 1966 the government said margarine should be consumed by the armed forces. Margarine had won the political support of the cotton and soybean farmers as the dairy front collapsed.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7, pp.289–290 (‘Out into the open sea’).

entries.label: The International Olive Oil Council is founded under UN auspices
entries.hint: The International Olive Council (originally the International Olive Oil Council), an intergovernmental body set up under the United Nations in 1959, aims to give growers and millers aid and advice, to fund research on oil quality and chemistry, and to promote consumption — and sets the trade standards for olive oil that the US, in 2010, still only voluntarily adopted.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history, glossary entry): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), glossary (‘IOC – International Olive Council, an intergovernmental agency instituted by the United Nations in 1959’), and the later chapters on the USDA standards of October 2010.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Crisco’s launch and the Blue Band slogan

entries.label: Crisco’s national launch: 1911–1912
entries.hint: To sell housewives on replacing lard, Procter & Gamble ran what was probably the most ambitious product launch yet attempted: the name Crisco was approved in April 1911, the J. Walter Thompson agency (Stanley Resor and copywriter Helen Lansdowne) tested eight alternative promotion plans in test cities, samples went to nutritionists and home economists, and in January 1912 every grocer in the United States was sent a case before a saturation national campaign. It sold an ‘all-vegetable’ shortening, not a soap or a candle.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dyer, Dalzell & Olegario, Rising Tide (2004) ch.2, pp.50–52 (PDF pp.64–65). Compare Schleifer, ‘The Perfect Solution’, Technology and Culture 53 (2012) on whether Crisco founded the trans-fat age.

entries.label: “Nut Lard”: coconut fat sold as a better lard
entries.hint: A British advertisement of 1912 offered ‘Nut Lard’, ‘an absolutely pure vegetable fat, extracted from the coco-nut … sweeter than ordinary lard or butter, and cheaper than either’, white, odourless and not liable to turn rancid, and ‘unequalled for frying fish’ because it did not splutter and could be strained and kept. It sits beside Crisco in the American launch of the same years as a sign of vegetable fats entering the kitchen.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter quoting an advertisement): Kiple (2000) II.E.2 p.390 (PDF p.427), citing the advertisement as Anon. 1912 pp.41–42, in Harries’s account of coconut oil and the fish-and-chip shop.

entries.label: Blue Band: “just like the best butter”
entries.loc: The Netherlands and the United Kingdom
entries.hint: In the Netherlands Blue Band margarine was advertised in the 1920s as ‘just like the best butter’; margarine advertisements elsewhere stressed ‘creamy richness’ and ‘made in the milky way’. Later laws in both countries banned such claims, though the United Kingdom still allows the slogan of one brand, ‘most people can’t tell the difference’. By the 1930s margarine was being advertised largely on its own merits.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Tousley, in van Stuyvenberg (ed.), Margarine (1969) pp.261–262, citing advertisements in Snodgrass and others. The decade is that of the Blue Band quotation.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Keys’s hypothesis, Kummerow’s trans-fat warning and the AHA’s 1961 report

entries.label: Ancel Keys’s diet–heart hypothesis
entries.hint: In 1952, at a presentation at Mount Sinai in New York, the physiologist Ancel Keys formally introduced his ‘diet-heart hypothesis’, tracing a line from dietary fat to blood cholesterol to heart disease, on a graph of fat intake against death rates from degenerative heart disease in six countries. His 1953 paper in the Journal of Mount Sinai Hospital published it. Teicholz calls this ‘the acorn’ from which mistrust of fat grew; the Berkeley biostatistician Jacob Yerushalmy, who heard Keys at a WHO conference in Geneva in 1955, thought the data looked ‘fishy’, since Geneva’s population ate a great deal of animal fat without dying of heart disease at high rates.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Teicholz, The Big Fat Surprise (2014) ch.2 (Keys’s chart, ‘Atherosclerosis: A Problem in Newer Public Health’, Journal of Mount Sinai Hospital 20(2) (July–August 1953) p.134). Yerushalmy’s doubts are from Teicholz’s account of the Geneva meeting, not checked against his own papers; Teicholz is a polemical source on this subject, and the diet–heart hypothesis is contested; see fats-1960-today.

entries.label: Kummerow studies trans fats in rats: the first warnings
entries.hint: The biochemist Fred Kummerow’s study of 1957, published in 1958 by Johnston, Johnson and Kummerow in the Journal of Nutrition, showed trans fatty acids depositing in rat tissues; he went on to warn that trans fats, produced by hydrogenation, behave like foreign agents in the body. Teicholz presents him as a lone voice against the industry and the Heart Association.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read; the studies not read): Teicholz (2014) ch.8 and notes — Johnston, Johnson & Kummerow, ‘Deposition in Tissues and Fecal Excretion of Trans Fatty Acids in the Rat’, Journal of Nutrition 65(1) (1958) pp.13–23. Her reading of Kummerow as vindicated is contested by those who defend the AHA’s caution on saturated fat.

entries.label: The AHA recommends a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet
entries.hint: In 1961 the American Heart Association’s Central Committee published its report ‘Dietary Fat and Its Relation to Heart Attacks and Strokes’ (JAMA, 4 February 1961), the first time a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet was officially recommended to the public. About one adult American in seven was then obese; Teicholz says forty years later it was one in three, with vegetable oils grown from zero to nearly 8 per cent of all calories consumed.
entries.note: SECONDARY (journalistic account read): Teicholz (2014) introduction and ch.2, and her bibliography (‘Central Committee for Medical and Community Program, American Heart Association, JAMA 175 (4 February 1961) pp.389–391’). Whether the rise in obesity follows from the advice is her argument, not an established fact.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Lever and whale oil, Unilever, margarine’s shifting fats, Wesson and Decatur, the palm plantations

entries.label: The first oil-palm plantations: Sumatra, 1911, and Malaya
entries.loc: Bangun Bandar, Deli, Sumatra and Malaya
entries.hint: The oil palm reached Southeast Asia about 1848, when four seedlings from Réunion and Amsterdam went to the Botanical Gardens at Bogor in Java as ornamentals for tobacco estates. The Belgian banker Adrien Hallet, rich from rubber and oil palm in the Congo, made the first oil-palm plantings in Sumatra in 1911, at Bangun Bandar in Deli — Indonesia’s first commercial oil-palm ventures — and the Frenchman Henri Fauconnier, in Malaya, founded his own company with Hallet’s backing and planted oil-palm seedlings Hallet gave him. The industry has been transnational from the start.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history and a collected volume): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021) ch.2 (the Bogor seedlings, Hallet 1909 and 1911, Fauconnier); Pye & Bhattacharya (eds), The Palm Oil Controversy in Southeast Asia (2013) conclusion (PDF p.252: ‘the first oil palm monoculture in North Sumatra in 1911’). Fauconnier’s first Malayan oil-palm planting date is not given in the passage read.

entries.label: Soy in America: from Wesson’s oil to the Decatur crushing plant
entries.hint: Cottonseed oil, sold as Wesson Oil after David Wesson developed a clarifying method in 1899, held back soybean oil in the United States until cottonseed oil became scarce in 1915; a soybean-processing plant opened at Decatur, Illinois, in 1922, with the ‘Peoria Plan’ guaranteeing Illinois farmers a base price of $1.35 a bushel. Research in the 1930s on refining, flavour reversion and hydrogenation resolved soybean oil’s remaining problems, and in 1938 the government opened its Regional Soybean Industrial Products Laboratory.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.5 p.424 (PDF p.461). The chapter dates the tariff duties to the ‘Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1923’, which looks wrong (that act is of 1930) and is not repeated here.

entries.label: Lever buys the Solomon Islands: a 999-year lease for coconut plantations, 1901–1907
entries.hint: After seeing his copra oil mill and soap factory at Balmain in Sydney in 1901, where coconut oil competed with tallow, Lever was drawn into a Pacific venture; he may have foreseen that rising consumption of oils and fats, above all by Europe’s margarine makers, would raise prices. In 1903 an interest group had a 99-year certificate of occupation for 193,490 acres in the Solomons; Lever bought the rights in 1906 for £5,000, and his agent Meek had bought about 51,000 acres of supposed freehold, 28,870 acres from islanders and 12,000 acres under occupancy certificates. In 1907 the lease became 999 years. A Colonial Office minute remarked that it was not every day that a millionaire became a tenant in the Solomons. Lever’s Pacific Plantations became one of Lever’s only two plantation companies until the 1920s, with the Belgian Congo’s.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Fieldhouse (1978) ch.8, ‘Lever’s Pacific Plantations Ltd.’, PDF pp.232–237; the plantation count is from ch.1, PDF p.37. The acreages and prices are Fieldhouse’s; islanders appear only as sellers and, later, as ‘native labour’ in his tables.

entries.label: Lever is refused West Africa and turns to the Congo
entries.loc: British West Africa and the Belgian Congo
entries.hint: In 1907 William Lever sought large-scale land concessions in the British West African colonies to produce palm oil for his Lancashire soap mills, but the Colonial Office, finding the region’s small, fragmented, often communally owned farms hard to administer and the scheme politically risky and commercially unsound, would not help. West Africa’s palm oil stayed in smallholders’ hands, and Lever took his plans to the Belgian Congo, whose administration welcomed European enterprise; his concessions there were granted in 1911 and his first investments brought heavy losses.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.3 p.397–398 (PDF p.435), citing Hancock 1942, Wilson 1954 and Fieldhouse 1978 pp.507–509.

entries.label: Lever’s Congo: the Huileries du Congo Belge, 1911
entries.hint: In 1911 Lever Brothers set up the Huileries du Congo Belge (HCB), ‘a vast and partially romantic project for exploiting and developing the raw materials of Equatorial Africa’, a trading company, SEDEC, followed in 1913, started trading in the Congo in 1916 and was first intended to buy and export palm oil and palm kernels. In West Africa the policy on concessions was disputed between liberal officials and what Hancock called ‘the soap boilers of the world’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (company history; chapter not read in full): Fieldhouse, Unilever Overseas (1978) ch.9 ‘Huileries du Congo Belge’ (contents PDF p.3) and ch.7, p.380 (PDF p.196) for the opening description and SEDEC and Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (2020 ed.) PDF p.282. Treat the detail of HCB’s operations as unchecked.

entries.label: Northern Nigeria’s groundnuts take off when the railway reaches Kano, 1911
entries.hint: Hopkins writes that the groundnut industry of northern Nigeria increased rapidly once the Lagos railway reached Kano in 1911, and that it had precolonial roots: groundnuts had long been grown in the region, and the initiative to expand them came from Hausa traders seeking to compensate for the decline of regional and trans-Saharan trade, who put their slaves to groundnut farming, only for the slaves to escape and farm on their own account. Elsewhere in West Africa, he adds, indigenous initiative created the cocoa farms of the Gold Coast and Nigeria and the groundnut farms of Senegal, and expanded exports of palm products from the forests.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (2020 ed.), PDF pp.47–48. The figures for Senegalese groundnuts (an average of 29,000 tons a year in 1886–90) and Lagos palm kernels (37,000 tons) are on PDF p.192 and belong to the 1850–1900 folio.

entries.label: Copra and glycerine: the Pacific coconut as war material, 1914–1942
entries.loc: The Pacific islands, the Philippines and Indonesia
entries.hint: The coconut palm was first grown as a plantation crop in the 1840s because industrial soap making needed cheap oil, and between 1846 and 1867 dynamite turned glycerine, once a discarded by-product of soap, into a profitable war material. After the First World War the German plantation territories in Africa and the Pacific were taken as reparation, and Japan administered the Caroline, Mariana and Marshall islands; in 1942 it added the Philippines and Indonesia, which then accounted for more than half the world’s copra.
entries.note: SECONDARY (encyclopedia chapter): Kiple (2000) the coconut chapter p.394 (PDF p.431), after Harries 1978. The chapter dates the plantation start and the dynamite years but gives the 1914–1942 span only by implication, so it is the folio’s bracket.

entries.label: Margarine’s fats change in a generation: coconut, then cottonseed, then soy
entries.hint: In the First World War, shortage of home-supplied animal fats and the new hardening process (introduced into the US from Europe in 1915) opened the way to imported vegetable oils; coconut oil accounted for as much as 75 per cent of US margarine raw materials in 1932, but only 8.5 per cent by 1940 as cottonseed oil’s processing was mastered and soybean growing grew. By 1943 margarine fat was 50 per cent cottonseed, 40 per cent soybean and 7 per cent animal fat; by 1966, 74 per cent soybean. The margarine industry became a recognised market for two of America’s great staple crops.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7, pp.288–289 (he dates the hardening of oils in the US to 1915, ‘introduced from Europe’, although Crisco was launched in 1911 — a discrepancy within the sources). Kiple II.E.5 p.424 gives the parallel soybean story (Wesson’s cottonseed oil from 1899, the 1915 cottonseed shortage, the Decatur plant of 1922, the Peoria Plan).

entries.label: Lever buys the world’s whale oil
entries.hint: In 1919 Lever Brothers bought the entire world production of whale oil and acquired the Southern Whaling Company, what the historian Gordon Jackson calls ‘vertical integration’: the soap maker controlled the market and could kill as many whales as it needed. Lever had earlier bought up the Testrup hardening patent, a rival to Normann’s, and half of the Norwegian hardening firm De-No-Fa; whale oil’s old unpopularity for soap, spread by the dairy interests’ ‘cadaver fats’ campaign, had faded by 1914.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.345–346 (PDF pp.368–369), citing Gordon Jackson. The figure of ‘the entire world production’ is Ellis’s phrase.

entries.label: Oil-palm hectares in Sumatra and Malaya, 1919–1938
entries.hint: More than 6,000 hectares had been planted with oil palm in Sumatra by 1919 and 32,000 by 1925, when Malaya had 3,400; Malaya added 17,000 more over the next five years while Sumatra’s area doubled, and by 1938 Malaya had nearly 30,000 hectares and Sumatra over 90,000. The expansion followed confidence in the palm and the grave postwar problems of the rubber industry, from which planters sought diversification; Deli Dura palms, descended from only four parents, gave uniform yields and the new setting lacked the palm’s usual pests.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.398–399 (PDF p.436), citing Lim 1967, Creutzberg 1975 and Hartley 1988.

entries.label: Lever’s Apapa soap works in Nigeria: 264 tons in 1924, over 3,000 in 1929
entries.hint: Lever’s West African Oil Company reopened its palm-kernel mills in 1916, when the war shut out the German kernel crushers of Hamburg and kernel oil prices rose, and closed them again in 1920 in the slump. Soap-making began at Apapa in 1923–24, and sales rose from 264 tons in 1924 to 3,143 tons in 1929, fell to 1,127 in 1934 in the Depression and reached 4,400 tons in 1937. Fieldhouse calls the Nigerian and Congo soap companies of the 1920s special cases, not part of a plan to manufacture in tropical Africa; Africa here is a manufacturer, as well as a supplier of kernels.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Fieldhouse (1978) ch.6, ‘Unilever in Black Africa’, PDF pp.177–179 (Table 6.1) and ch.1, PDF p.16. The soap tonnages are those of the company’s own record as Fieldhouse tabulates them.

entries.label: Turkey in 1939: Atatürk’s duties end the fat imports, and a Unilever survey finds a market
entries.hint: A Unilever report of 1939 found Turkey a country of 16–17 million people being modernised under a government that welcomed private enterprise. Margarine imports had been a mere 900 kg in 1923; in the 1920s Kemal Atatürk’s government imposed heavy duties and the import trade in edible fats, mainly vegetable ghee, was virtually destroyed. Van den Bergh’s men thought a market could be created for about 1,500 tons of margarine and 1,000 tons of ghee substitute beside the existing market for butter and ghee. A local firm, Turyag, owned an oil mill, refinery, hardening plant, margarine and soap factories at Izmir and claimed to control 75 per cent of organised oil sales in Turkey.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Sheila Fieldhouse’s chapter ‘Unilever in Turkey’ in Fieldhouse (1978), PDF pp.215–216. The market estimates are Unilever’s 1939 projection, not an outcome; Turyag’s 75 per cent is the firm’s own claim as reported there.

entries.label: Pelagic whaling: the stern slipway, and the 1930–31 slaughter
entries.hint: In 1925 the Norwegian factory ship Lancing was equipped with a stern slipway that let whales be hauled aboard and processed anywhere, forcing the British to refit their whole pelagic fleet. By 1930–31 Norwegian and British fleets were ‘promethean floating industries’: tankers of over 10,000 tons with stern slipways, digesters, pressure cookers and crews of over five hundred, and the 1930–31 season saw the greatest slaughter of blue whales in history. In 1929 the cost of the southern fleet strained Lever Brothers’ resources and it merged with the Margarine Union to form Unilever.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.346–347 (PDF pp.369–370). That the fleet’s cost pressed Lever into the merger is Ellis’s statement; Jones, Renewing Unilever (2005) Introduction (PDF p.26) gives the merger date and constituents only.

entries.label: Lever Brothers and the Margarine Union form Unilever
entries.hint: Unilever was created in 1929 by a merger of the British Lever Brothers, pioneer of branded soap, and the Dutch Margarine Unie, itself a merger of the leading Dutch margarine makers including Van den Bergh and Jurgens, Hartog’s meat business at Oss and the central European Schicht. Soap and margarine, both made from the same fats and oils, shaped the firm; after 1929 margarine production began in several countries.
entries.note: ANCHOR (two books read): Jones, Renewing Unilever (2005) Introduction, PDF p.26 (‘Unilever’s Origins’); Fieldhouse, Unilever Overseas (1978) PDF p.13 (margarine production begun in several countries after 1929) and p.24.

entries.label: India’s vanaspati: from a ghee additive to 43,000 tons in 1941
entries.hint: After the tariff of 1931–32 protected local manufacturers, the Van den Bergh-Lever business in India, Hindustan Vanaspati Manufacturing, saw vanaspati sales rise from 11,222 tons in 1935 to 43,065 tons in 1941, while its soap sales rose from 9,897 to 20,040 tons. Vanaspati began as an additive to ghee and only gradually became a product in its own right after 1939; sold in bulk, it could not be a branded product. The company’s share of the market, high because it was among the first in the field, fell to 40.9 per cent by 1943 and 23.7 per cent by 1949, as Indian entrepreneurs, seeing how profitable it was, moved in. Indian raw materials were no cheaper: in the 1930s vegetable oils cost less at Port Sunlight or Rotterdam than in Bombay or Calcutta.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Fieldhouse, Unilever Overseas (1978) ch.4, ‘Unilever in India and Pakistan’, PDF pp.93–94 (Tables 4.4 and 4.5). Compare fats-1960-today::ec8 for the 1960s price controls on vanaspati.

entries.label: Southeast Asia overtakes Nigeria: palm oil in the 1930s
entries.loc: The Netherlands East Indies, Nigeria and Malaya
entries.hint: By 1934 the Netherlands East Indies had replaced Nigeria as the world’s major palm oil exporter: from 1934 to 1938 the NEI’s exports averaged 171,000 tonnes a year, Nigeria’s 137,000, and Malaya’s only 34,000. The Malayan industry was small, though United Plantations and its sister company Bernam Oil Palms, in the Westenholz family’s hands, had been growing since 1917.
entries.note: ANCHOR (company history read): Martin, The UP Saga (2003) ch.4 (PDF p.84; ‘SURVIVAL AND GROWTH IN THE PALM OIL INDUSTRY’), with Table 1 on planted area and output, 1917–40. The Westenholz detail is from the same chapter.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Hydrogenation, Crisco and the factory ship

entries.label: The factory ship and the grenade harpoon
entries.hint: Svend Foyn’s grenade harpoon fired from a cannon, invented about 1865–67 and perfected through the 1870s, let whalers kill the fast rorquals the earlier hand-harpoon fishery could not catch; ‘probably the most enduring and pernicious’ invention in the history of whaling. Norwegians began Antarctic shore whaling at Grytviken (1904) and floating factories followed from 1905; the stern slipway of 1925 made the factory ship independent of the land.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.255–262 (PDF pp.280–285), p.263 and 265 (Salvesen, the Admiralen in 1905), p.342 (PDF p.365; Grytviken) and pp.346–347. Ellis gives the invention as ‘around 1865’ in one place and 1867 in another.

entries.label: Normann’s hydrogenation patents and the first hardening plant
entries.hint: Wilhelm Normann introduced hydrogen into liquid oils in the presence of a catalyst: his German patent no. 141,029 was filed on 14 August 1902 (issued 4 May 1903) for the Herforder Maschinenfett, and his British patent no. 1,515, applied for on 21 January 1903, was accepted on 26 November 1903; the patent names olive oil, linseed oil and whale oil. By 1906 whale oil was being hydrogenated for margarine, and the first large-scale hydrogenation plant began work at Crosfield’s works in Warrington. The value of hardening was only appreciated about 1908–09, and whale oil was fully brought under control only about 1930.
entries.note: ANCHOR (annotated bibliography read, quoting the patents): Aoyagi, History of Hydrogenation, Shortening and Margarine (PDF pp.5, 47–48), citing Weber & Alsberg 1934 and Schwitzer 1956; Hunt in van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.2 p.64 on the timing. Sabatier and Senderens’s earlier work on vapour-phase hydrogenation is acknowledged in Normann’s British patent.

entries.label: The Tenera palm: a hybrid that revolutionised yields
entries.hint: In 1902 the Germans in Kamerun identified an exceptionally thin-shelled palm with a high oil content, the ‘lisombe’, later the Tenera, but it was rare and did not breed true; the Belgians began investigating in 1922, with an experimental plantation at Yangambi in the Congo. M. Beirnaert showed in tests of the 1930s, published in 1941, that Tenera is a hybrid of the thick-shelled Dura and the shell-less Pisifera, and when self-pollinated yields 50 per cent Tenera, 25 per cent Dura and 25 per cent Pisifera; large-scale Tenera breeding began only after 1945, and the new planting materials sharply raised yields and cut costs.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.398 (PDF p.436), citing Hartley 1988 and Beirnaert & Vanderweyen 1941. The chapter says the Congo was ironically not the state that gained most from it.

entries.label: Crisco: Kayser’s hydrogenation and an “all-vegetable” lard
entries.hint: In 1907 an independent scientist, E. C. Kayser, approached Procter & Gamble with a hydrogenation technique that turned liquid oils into solid fats; a research team led by Morrison and M. B. ‘Doc’ Graff worked in secret, and by 1910 had a patentable edible shortening of cottonseed oil mixed with cottonseed stearin, first called Krispo, launched in 1911 as Crisco. P&G had formed the Buckeye cotton-oil company in 1903 to secure supplies. The American Heart Association and some journalists date the birth of trans fats to Crisco, but Schleifer argues it fitted the long-established class of ‘compound lards’ and changed it by stressing purity.
entries.note: ANCHOR (two works read): Dyer et al., Rising Tide (2004) ch.1–2 (PDF pp.60, 64) and Schleifer, ‘The Perfect Solution: How Trans Fats Became the Healthy Replacement for Saturated Fats’, Technology and Culture 53(1) (2012) pp.94–119. The relation of Kayser’s process to Normann’s patents is not discussed in the passages read.

entries.label: Manchurian soy goes to Europe
entries.hint: Japan imported soybean cake as fertiliser from the early 1900s, and the first shipments of whole soybeans to Europe are reported about 1908. The very large Manchurian export trade owed something to the Russo-Japanese war of 1904–05, whose demand for food to feed Japanese troops left a surplus when they were withdrawn, and grew under immigrant labour to a peak in the 1920s and early 1930s; the crop did well in the United States, which expanded it when the Second World War cut off other supplies.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Hunt, ‘The raw materials’, in van Stuyvenberg (ed.), Margarine (1969) ch.2 (the passage on soya bean). The Russo-Japanese link is Hunt’s probable explanation (‘probably due in part’).

entries.label: The depression and the glut of oils and fats
entries.hint: The world depression brought a glut of oils and fats: a million more tons of oilseed crops were grown in the mid-1930s than in the previous decade, whale oil output doubled, and governments answered with tariffs and imperial preference (see o2); the margarine makers’ raw materials were repeatedly rearranged by prices and politics.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Hunt in van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.2 (the 1929–33 passage). The doubling of whale oil is in the same passage as the oilseed figures.
